title: How do you configure a Spring Boot application to use two databases, with separate DataSource, EntityManagerFactory and TransactionManager for each?
shortTitle: How do you connect to two databases in Spring Boot?

s1_definition.profdef: To use two databases in one Spring Boot app you give up auto-configuration and define, for EACH database, three beans: a `DataSource` (connection details and pool), a `LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean` (the JPA factory scanning that database's entity package), and a `PlatformTransactionManager` (bound to that factory). You mark ONE set as `@Primary` so ambiguous injections resolve. Each database's entities and repositories live in SEPARATE packages, and you point Spring Data at them with `@EnableJpaRepositories(basePackages = ..., entityManagerFactoryRef = ..., transactionManagerRef = ...)`. Repositories for database A are created against factory A and use transaction manager A; repositories for database B use factory B and transaction manager B. A single `@Transactional` spans only ONE database unless you add a distributed/XA transaction manager; by default each database has its own local transaction, so cross-database atomicity is not guaranteed without XA or a saga.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India keeps core accounts in one vault (the primary database) and audit/compliance records in a separate vault (the secondary database). Each vault has its own key (DataSource), its own filing clerk who knows only that vault's layout (EntityManagerFactory), and its own supervisor who signs off deposits and withdrawals for that vault (TransactionManager). You tell each department which vault, clerk, and supervisor to use. One supervisor's sign-off covers only their own vault; coordinating a change across both vaults needs a higher authority (XA) or a careful two-step plan (saga).
s1_definition.oneliner: For two databases, define per-database DataSource + EntityManagerFactory + TransactionManager, keep entities/repositories in separate packages wired with `@EnableJpaRepositories(entityManagerFactoryRef, transactionManagerRef)`, mark one `@Primary`, and remember a plain `@Transactional` is atomic within ONE database only.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** To use two databases in one Spring Boot app you give up auto-configuration and define, for EACH database, three beans: a `DataSource` (connection details and pool), a `LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean` (the JPA factory scanning that database's entity package), and a `PlatformTransactionManager` (bound to that factory). You mark ONE set as `@Primary` so ambiguous injections resolve. Each database's entities and repositories live in SEPARATE packages, and you point Spring Data at them with `@EnableJpaRepositories(basePackages = ..., entityManagerFactoryRef = ..., transactionManagerRef = ...)`. Repositories for database A are created against factory A and use transaction manager A; repositories for database B use factory B and transaction manager B. A single `@Transactional` spans only ONE database unless you add a distributed/XA transaction manager; by default each database has its own local transaction, so cross-database atomicity is not guaranteed without XA or a saga.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India keeps core accounts in one vault (the primary database) and audit/compliance records in a separate vault (the secondary database). Each vault has its own key (DataSource), its own filing clerk who knows only that vault's layout (EntityManagerFactory), and its own supervisor who signs off deposits and withdrawals for that vault (TransactionManager). You tell each department which vault, clerk, and supervisor to use. One supervisor's sign-off covers only their own vault; coordinating a change across both vaults needs a higher authority (XA) or a careful two-step plan (saga).

**One line to remember:** For two databases, define per-database DataSource + EntityManagerFactory + TransactionManager, keep entities/repositories in separate packages wired with `@EnableJpaRepositories(entityManagerFactoryRef, transactionManagerRef)`, mark one `@Primary`, and remember a plain `@Transactional` is atomic within ONE database only.

sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the real split at National Bank of India that required two databases.

Problem 1 — core banking and audit had different databases and owners. Core account data lived in the main transactional database owned by the banking team, while an immutable audit/compliance log lived in a separate database owned by the compliance team, often on different hardware with different backup policies. One service needed to write to both. This is exactly the two-database case: each needs its own DataSource, EntityManagerFactory, and TransactionManager.

Problem 2 — entities and repositories kept colliding. An early attempt put all entities in one package, and Hibernate tried to map audit entities against the core database. This is exactly why each database needs its own entity package and its own `@EnableJpaRepositories` wiring, so the core factory scans only core entities and the audit factory scans only audit entities.

Problem 3 — a cross-database write left the systems inconsistent. A method updated a core account and then wrote an audit record; when the audit write failed, the account change had already committed. This is exactly the no-cross-database-atomicity caveat: two local transactions are not one atomic unit. The project records the decision to either use XA for true atomicity or, as chosen here, keep each write in its own transaction and design the audit write to be retried safely.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There are two config classes, `CoreJpaConfig` and `AuditJpaConfig`, each defining a DataSource, an EntityManagerFactory, and a TransactionManager, with the core set marked `@Primary`. The core database has an `Account` entity and repository in the core package; the audit database has an `AuditRecord` entity and repository in the audit package. The `BankingService` writes an account change under the core transaction manager and writes an audit record under the audit transaction manager, with a clear comment that these are two separate transactions. A test verifies the two transaction managers and factories are distinct beans. (The config uses property prefixes so the two databases are independently configured.)

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package

# Run (expects coredb on 5432 and auditdb on 5433)
java -jar target/multidb-banking-service-1.0.0.jar

# Debit — writes to coredb AND auditdb in TWO separate transactions
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8370/api/v1/banking/SAV2001/debit?amount=50000"
# coredb:  UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-50000 WHERE account_id='SAV2001'  (coreTransactionManager)
# auditdb: INSERT INTO audit_records (account_id, action, detail) VALUES ('SAV2001','DEBIT',...)  (auditTransactionManager)

# Run tests
mvn test
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is debiting 50000 from Rajesh's account and writing an audit record.

Step 1 — startup wiring. Spring reads the two datasource prefixes. `CoreJpaConfig` builds the core DataSource (pointing at coredb), the core EntityManagerFactory (scanning only the core entity package), and the core TransactionManager, all marked `@Primary`. `AuditJpaConfig` builds the audit equivalents (pointing at auditdb, scanning only the audit entity package), qualified by name. The core repositories are created against the core factory; the audit repositories against the audit factory.

Step 2 — debit. `debitWithAudit` calls `debit(...)`, which is `@Transactional("coreTransactionManager")`. A transaction opens on coredb only. Hibernate loads the account from coredb, subtracts 50000, and on commit issues `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50000 WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001'` against coredb. This transaction commits and closes.

Step 3 — audit. `debitWithAudit` then calls `audit(...)`, which is `@Transactional("auditTransactionManager")`. A SEPARATE transaction opens on auditdb. The audit repository inserts a row into `audit_records` in auditdb, and that transaction commits.

Step 4 — the two transactions are independent. The debit committed in coredb before the audit transaction even began. There is no single atomic unit spanning both databases. If the audit write failed, the debit would already be committed; the design handles this by making the audit write retry-safe rather than assuming rollback.

Step 5 — if true atomicity were required, I would introduce an XA/JTA transaction manager to coordinate a two-phase commit across both databases, accepting its performance and operational cost, or I would use a saga/outbox pattern for eventual consistency. The project explicitly records this trade-off.

```
2026-10-24 00:57:55 INFO  BankingService - [coreTransactionManager] debited Rs.50000 from SAV2001 (coredb)
2026-10-24 00:57:55 FINE  BankingService - coredb COMMIT (transaction 1 closed)
2026-10-24 00:57:55 INFO  BankingService - [auditTransactionManager] wrote audit for SAV2001 (auditdb)
2026-10-24 00:57:55 INFO  BankingService - Completed debit+audit — two independent transactions (consider XA/saga)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Client: POST /api/v1/banking/SAV2001/debit?amount=50000
    │
    ▼
  BankingController → BankingService.debitWithAudit(...)
    │
    ├─ debit(...)  @Transactional("coreTransactionManager")
    │    coreDataSource → coreEntityManagerFactory(core.model) → coreTransactionManager
    │    UPDATE accounts SET balance=balance-50000 → COREDB  ──COMMIT (txn 1)
    │
    └─ audit(...) @Transactional("auditTransactionManager")
         auditDataSource → auditEntityManagerFactory(audit.model) → auditTransactionManager
         INSERT audit_records → AUDITDB  ──COMMIT (txn 2)

  ── PER-DATABASE TRIO ──
  CORE  (primary): coreDataSource  + coreEntityManagerFactory  + coreTransactionManager
  AUDIT (secondary): auditDataSource + auditEntityManagerFactory + auditTransactionManager
  @EnableJpaRepositories wires each repository package to its own factory + txn manager

  ── ATOMICITY ──
  plain @Transactional → ONE database only (two local transactions here)
  cross-DB atomic      → needs XA/JTA (2-phase commit) OR saga/outbox (eventual consistency)
```

```
  ═══ LLD — Multi-DataSource JPA Config (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Multiple Bean Trios: DataSource/EMF/TxnManager per database       │
  │  Package Partitioning: entities+repos isolated per DB              │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: each config class owns exactly one database's wiring          │
  │  D: services depend on repository interfaces, not on datasources  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Bean Graph ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  @Primary coreDataSource ─▶ coreEntityManagerFactory(core.model) ─▶ coreTransactionManager
                                                                  ▲
        @EnableJpaRepositories(core.repository, emf=core, txn=core)┘

         auditDataSource ─▶ auditEntityManagerFactory(audit.model) ─▶ auditTransactionManager
                                                                   ▲
        @EnableJpaRepositories(audit.repository, emf=audit, txn=audit)┘

  ── Call Chain (debit+audit) ──
  1. debitWithAudit()
  2.   debit()  @Transactional("coreTransactionManager")  → COMMIT coredb
  3.   audit()  @Transactional("auditTransactionManager") → COMMIT auditdb

  (Caution) Two local transactions ≠ one atomic unit; failure after step 2 leaves inconsistency.
  Rule: define the trio per DB, mark one @Primary, qualify the rest; use XA/saga for cross-DB atomicity.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To use two databases in one Spring Boot application I give up single-database auto-configuration and define, for each database, three beans: a DataSource with its own connection details and pool, a LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean that scans only that database's entity package, and a PlatformTransactionManager bound to that factory. I keep each database's entities and repositories in separate packages and wire them with EnableJpaRepositories pointing at the correct entityManagerFactoryRef and transactionManagerRef. I mark one database's beans as Primary so that ambiguous by-type injections resolve, and I qualify the other database's beans by name. The result is that core repositories run against the core factory and core transaction manager, and audit repositories run against the audit factory and audit transaction manager.

In our banking service at National Bank of India, core account data lives in the main transactional database owned by the banking team and an immutable audit log lives in a separate database owned by compliance. The service debits an account under the core transaction manager and writes an audit record under the audit transaction manager. Keeping the entities in separate packages is essential, because otherwise Hibernate would try to map audit entities against the core database.

The most important correctness point I always raise is transaction scope. A plain Transactional method commits against exactly one transaction manager, hence one database, so when a single operation writes to both databases those are two independent local transactions, not one atomic unit. If the second write fails after the first commits, the two systems are inconsistent. To make a single operation atomic across both databases I need a distributed XA or JTA transaction manager that coordinates a two-phase commit, which carries real performance and operational costs, so in practice I often avoid cross-database transactions entirely and design for eventual consistency with a saga or an outbox pattern, making the second write retry-safe rather than assuming it can be rolled back with the first.
